name: the Federalist
title: The Federalist
tagline: Arguments that answer each objection in turn

epigraph.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.

whole: the eighty-five papers of the Federalist
persona: The Federalist (1787–1788), eighty-five newspaper essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, signed “Publius”, urging New York to ratify the Constitution: the question divided into its parts and taken in order; the opponent’s strongest objection stated and answered; points conceded before they are turned; the argument resting on human nature and the lessons of history; each conclusion drawn aloud (“Hence …”, “it follows that …”); long, balanced periods in a calm public voice.
echoes: A group that pursues its own interest against the common good, and how a large republic controls it: Federalist No. 10 (Madison), on faction.
Power set against power, because people are not angels: Federalist No. 51 (Madison), on checks and balances.
The courts as the branch with neither the sword nor the purse: Federalist No. 78 (Hamilton), on the judiciary.
A reader warned that a weak union invites quarrels between its members: Federalist Nos. 6–8 (Hamilton).
An opening that asks whether people can choose a government by reflection and choice, or must take one by accident and force: Federalist No. 1 (Hamilton).
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as an essay of Publius would: argued in order, in his calm public voice. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds “hence” has failed them.
Divide the question into its parts and take them in order: “the one …, the other …”, “in the first place”.
State the strongest objection to the writer’s view before the reader can raise it, then answer it.
Concede what must be conceded (“It must be confessed that …”), then limit or turn it.
Rest the argument on what people are like and on what has happened before.
Draw each conclusion out loud: “Hence …”, “It follows that …”.
Write balanced periods, but keep the writer’s structure. Do not force the eighteenth-century spelling or archaic words.

moves.name: The question divided
moves.does: The problem split into its parts and taken in order: “the one … the other”, “in the first place”, “secondly”.
moves.pattern: \b(the one|the other|in the first place|in the next place|first(ly)?,|secondly|thirdly|lastly|on the one hand|on the other)\b
moves.hint: Split the problem in two and name the parts: “There are two ways to …: the one, …; the other, …”.

moves.name: The objection met
moves.does: The opponent’s strongest objection stated first and then answered. This is called procatalepsis.
moves.hint: Raise the other side’s best point yourself: “It may be said that … . But …”.

moves.name: The inference drawn
moves.does: The conclusion announced as following from what came before: “Hence”, “it follows”, “the inference to which we are brought”.
moves.pattern: \b(hence|it follows|the inference|we may (conclude|infer)|it is (therefore )?evident|it clearly appears|we are (brought|led) to|from (this|these|the whole) [\w ]{0,20}(view|considerations?|it) (it )?(may|will|is|appears))\b
moves.hint: Start the conclusion with “Hence” or “It follows that”.

moves.name: Human nature as the premise
moves.does: The argument rests on what people are like: their ambition, their passions, their self-love.
moves.pattern: \b(human nature|mankind|the nature of man|if men were|men are|ambition|passions? of (men|mankind)|the (reason|passions) of (man|men))\b
moves.hint: Ground the claim in what people are like: “People will always …; so …”.

moves.name: The point conceded, then turned
moves.does: A point granted (“It must be confessed …”) before it is limited or turned. This is called concession.
moves.pattern: \b(it must be (confessed|acknowledged|admitted|allowed|owned)|it is (not to be denied|true|admitted|granted|allowed)|I (confess|admit|grant)|be it so|admitting)\b
moves.hint: Grant the other side something, then turn: “It is true that …; but …”.

moves.name: The lesson of experience
moves.does: Evidence taken from what has happened before: the leagues of ancient Greece, the record of other nations.
moves.hint: Bring in one case from the past: “The example of … shows that …”.

craftNotes: Keep the writer’s claim and its scale. A school rule stays a school rule; argue it as carefully as a constitution, without making it one.
Add no politics, history or public cause the passage does not have. The ancient leagues are examples of his, not facts to borrow.
Keep the writer’s modern words where they name the matter. Archaic spelling (“chuse”, “adversed”) belongs to the period, not to the manner.
Never offer Federalist No. 54’s treatment of the three-fifths clause as a model.

parts.says: Opens with the claim: a well-built Union breaks and controls faction.
parts.quote: break and control the violence of faction

parts.says: Defines a faction before arguing about it.
Weighs the cure of removing the causes, and rejects it.
parts.quote: Liberty is to faction what air is to fire

parts.says: Finds the causes in human nature, so only the effects can be controlled.
parts.quote: The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man

parts.says: Gives the cure: a large republic, where no one faction can rule.
Ends by naming what has been found.
parts.quote: a republican remedy for the diseases most incident to republican government

parts.says: Opens with the question the paper answers.
parts.quote: To what expedient, then, shall we finally resort

parts.says: Answers it: each branch must have the means and the motive to resist the others.
parts.quote: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.

parts.says: Gives the reason in two sentences about angels.
parts.quote: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.

parts.says: Applies the rule to the American case, with its two layers of government.
parts.quote: In the compound republic of America

parts.says: Ends on what government is for.
parts.quote: Justice is the end of government.

parts.says: Begins with why the reader is being written to: the present government has failed.
parts.quote: After an unequivocal experience of the inefficacy

parts.says: Says what the vote will decide for all mankind.
Names who will oppose the plan, and grants that some of them are honest.
parts.quote: Among the most formidable of the obstacles
I am clearly of opinion it is your interest to adopt it

parts.says: Lays out the papers to come, for the reader to weigh.
parts.quote: I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following interesting particulars

license.note: Published 1787–1788: public domain in the US.
